label: thm:mechanism
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:mechanism}
Let $F\colon\mathbb P^2\to\mathbb P^2$ be a holomorphic endomorphism of algebraic degree
$d\ge2$ satisfying hypothesis
\hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)}.
Suppose that the fast direction is history-dependent.
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item If $\lambda_2\ge2\log d$, then
$\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_F=2\log d/\lambda_2$.
\item If $\log d<\lambda_2<2\log d$, then
$\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_F\ge1+(2\log d-\lambda_2)/\lambda_1$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, if $\lambda_2>\log d$, then
$\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_F-\mathcal D_{\mathrm{P}}(F)>0$.

label: thm:open
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{thm:open}
There exist constants $C>1$ and $B_0>0$ such that, for every pair of
real parameters $A,B$ satisfying $B>B_0$ and $CB<A<B^2/C$, the map
$F_{A,B}(z,w):=(z^2-A,w^2-B+z)$ satisfies
$\lambda_1(F_{A,B})>\lambda_2(F_{A,B})>\log4$ and
$$
 \dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_{F_{A,B}}
 =\frac{2\log2}{\lambda_2(F_{A,B})}>\mathcal D_{\mathrm{P}}(F_{A,B}).
$$

label: prop:holomorphic-leaves
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:holomorphic-leaves}
There are constants $r_*>0$ and $C_*<\infty$ such that, for every
$\hat x\in\hat K$, the ball $B(x_0,r_*)$ admits holomorphic
coordinates $(u,v)$ whose $v$-fibers are the local strong unstable
leaves associated with the inverse history of $\hat x$.
On a fixed smaller neighborhood, the coordinate maps and their
inverses have $C^2$ norms bounded by $C_*$.
The coordinates can be chosen continuously on each member of a
finite open cover of $\hat K$, and coordinates associated with
the same inverse history define the same foliation on overlaps.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After passing to a fixed iterate,
the domination estimate \eqref{eq:uniform-domination} gives uniform
contraction of slopes in the fast cones. This contraction persists
on complex neighborhoods whose radius is independent of the
history and the backward iterate. The inverse branches map these
neighborhoods into the corresponding backward neighborhoods.
Starting with a constant line field in the fast cone at a backward
iterate and transporting it forward along the prescribed history
gives holomorphic line fields converging locally uniformly,
with error at most $C\rho^n$ after $n$ graph transform steps,
where $C>0$ and $0<\rho<1$ are independent of the history.
The limit is independent of the initial field, depends continuously
on the history, and has value $E^f(\hat x)$ at $x_0$.
Its integral curves are the strong unstable leaves by uniqueness
of the graph transform.

For the fixed inverse history, write the limiting field in suitable
linear coordinates $(z,w)$ as $\operatorname{span}(1,\sigma(z,w))$,
where $\sigma$ is its holomorphic slope function.
Solving $dw/dz=\sigma(z,w)$ with initial values on a transverse
complex disk gives the required holomorphic flow box.
Uniform cone bounds and Cauchy estimates give uniform $C^2$ bounds
for the coordinates and their inverses after a fixed shrinking.
Choose the initial coordinates and transverse disks continuously
on each member of a finite open cover of $\hat K$.
Continuous dependence of the flow then gives continuous choices
of leaf coordinates, while uniqueness of the limiting line field
makes the foliations agree on overlaps for the same history.

label: lem:conditional-mass
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:conditional-mass}

Let $\nu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n$,
let $\zeta$ be its projection to the second factor, and write
$\nu=\int\nu_v\,d\zeta(v)$ 
for the disintegration of $\nu$ with respect to $\zeta$, so that $\nu_v$ is the conditional probability on
$\mathbb R^m\times\{v\}$, identified with a measure on $\mathbb R^m$.
Suppose $\underline d_{\nu_v}(y)\ge\alpha\ge0$ for
$\nu$-almost every $(y,v) \in \mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item
If $\nu$ is exact dimensional of dimension $D$, then
$\overline d_\zeta(v)\le D-\alpha$ for $\zeta$-almost every $v$.

\item
Suppose $\underline d_\zeta(v)\ge\beta\ge0$ for
$\zeta$-almost every $v$.
Fix $a,b>0$ and translation vectors $h_f\in\mathbb R^m$ and
$h_t\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$\mathcal R_k$ be the product partition $\mathcal D_{\lfloor ak\rfloor}^{h_f}
\times\mathcal D_{\lfloor bk\rfloor}^{h_t}$.
Then
$$
 \liminf_{k\to\infty}
 \frac{\log\nu(\mathcal R_k(x))}{-k\log2}
 \ge a\alpha+b\beta
 \qquad\text{for $\nu$-almost every $x$,}
$$
where $\mathcal R_k(x)$ is the element in the partition $\mathcal R_k$ containing $x$.
\end{enumerate}
Both (i) and (ii) remain valid under a bi-Lipschitz change
of local product coordinates preserving the fiber foliation,
with the product partition in (ii) pulled back under
the coordinate map.
head: environment

label: eq:conditional-mass-estimate
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\varepsilon>0$.
Since $\underline d_{\nu_v}(y)\ge\alpha\ge0$, there are measurable
sets $J_N$ increasing to full $\nu$-measure such that
$\nu_v(B(y,r))\le r^{\alpha-\varepsilon}$ whenever
$(y,v)\in J_N$ and $0<r<1/N$.
Suppose a Borel set $E$ has fiber sections of diameter at most
$r_f<1/(2N)$ and its projection to $\mathbb R^n$ is contained in a
ball $B_t$.
On each fiber meeting $J_N\cap E$, a ball of radius $2r_f$
centered at a point of that intersection contains the fiber
section of $E$.
Applying
$\nu_v(B(y,2r_f))\leq (2r_f)^{\alpha-\varepsilon}$
on each such fiber and integrating over $v\in B_t$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conditional-mass-estimate}
 \nu(J_N\cap E)
 \le C_\varepsilon r_f^{\alpha-\varepsilon}\zeta(B_t).
\end{equation}

\smallskip

For (i), the differentiation theorem for finite Borel measures
on Euclidean space gives
$\nu(J_N\cap B(x,r))/\nu(B(x,r))\to1$
as $r\to0$
for $\nu$-almost every $x\in J_N$.
Thus $\nu(B(x,r))\le2\nu(J_N\cap B(x,r))$ for
$\nu$-almost every $x=(y,v)\in J_N$ and all sufficiently
small $r$.
Applying \eqref{eq:conditional-mass-estimate}
with $E=B(x,r)$, $r_f=2r$, and $B_t=B(v,r)$ yields
$\nu(B(x,r))\le C_\varepsilon
r^{\alpha-\varepsilon}\zeta(B(v,r))$.
Exact dimensionality gives
$\nu(B(x,r))\ge r^{D+\varepsilon}$ for all sufficiently
small $r$, so
$\zeta(B(v,r))\ge C_\varepsilon^{-1}
r^{D-\alpha+2\varepsilon}$.
Hence $\overline d_\zeta(v)\le D-\alpha+2\varepsilon$
for $\nu$-almost every $(y,v)\in J_N$.
Taking the union over $N$, this inequality holds for
$\nu$-almost every $(y,v)$, hence for $\zeta$-almost every $v$,
since it depends only on $v$.
Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ along a countable sequence proves (i).

\smallskip

For (ii), let $\mathcal F_k:=\sigma(\mathcal R_k)$ be the
$\sigma$-algebra generated by the elements of $\mathcal R_k$.
These $\sigma$-algebras increase and together generate the Borel
$\sigma$-algebra. L\'evy's upward theorem
\cite[Section 14.2]{Williams1991} gives
$\mathbb E_\nu(\mathbf1_{J_N}\mid\mathcal F_k)\to\mathbf1_{J_N}$
$\nu$-almost everywhere, and therefore
$\nu(J_N\cap\mathcal R_k(x))/\nu(\mathcal R_k(x))\to1$
for $\nu$-almost every $x\in J_N$.
Thus
$\nu(\mathcal R_k(x))\le2\nu(J_N\cap\mathcal R_k(x))$
for $\nu$-almost every $x=(y,v)\in J_N$ and all sufficiently
large $k$.
Apply \eqref{eq:conditional-mass-estimate} with
$E=\mathcal R_k(x)$,
$r_f=C2^{-ak}$,
and $B_t=B(v,C2^{-bk})$, where $C$ depends
only on $m$ and $n$.
The assumption $\underline d_\zeta(v)\ge\beta$ gives
$\zeta(B_t)\le C_\varepsilon2^{-bk(\beta-\varepsilon)}$
for all sufficiently large $k$, depending on $v$.
Thus
$\nu(\mathcal R_k(x))
\le C_\varepsilon
2^{-k(a(\alpha-\varepsilon)+b(\beta-\varepsilon))}$.
Taking logarithms, then the lower limit, and finally the
union over $N$ and $\varepsilon\to0$ proves (ii).

\smallskip

For local product coordinates given by a bi-Lipschitz map $\Phi$
preserving the fiber foliation, apply the preceding argument
to the pushforward $\Phi_*\nu$.
The coordinate map and its restrictions to fibers preserve
local dimensions, and the partition elements in the original coordinates
are $\Phi^{-1}(\mathcal R_k(\Phi(x)))$.

label: prop:dimension
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:dimension}
Under \hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)}, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item
The equilibrium measure $\mu$ is exact dimensional, with
$\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu=h_1/\lambda_1+(2L-h_1)/\lambda_2$.

\item
The conditional measures on the fast leaves are exact
dimensional with dimension $h_1/\lambda_1$.

\item
In a history box
$\Theta((K\cap U)\times S)$ with $\mu(U)>0$ and
$\beta(S)>0$, for $\beta$-almost every $s\in S$ for which
$p_s$ is defined on $U$, the transverse measure
$(p_s)_*\mu_U$ is exact dimensional with dimension
$(2L-h_1)/\lambda_2$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, we have
$\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu-\mathcal D_{\mathrm{P}}(F)=(L-h_1)(\lambda_2^{-1}-\lambda_1^{-1})$
and $0\le h_1\le L$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $DF$ is non-singular on the compact set $K$, we have
$\log|\det D_{\mathbb R}F|\in L^1(\mu)$, as required in \cite{QianXie2008}.
Proposition 2.4 there gives exact conditional dimensions, and
equation (19), with $h_2=2L$, identifies them as
$\delta_f=h_1/\lambda_1$ and
$\delta_u=h_1/\lambda_1+(2L-h_1)/\lambda_2$
on the fast and full unstable leaves.
Under \hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)}, the $W^1$-manifolds of
\cite{QianXie2008} coincide locally with the strong fast leaves of
Proposition \ref{prop:holomorphic-leaves}, by uniqueness of the
strong unstable manifolds.

By \eqref{eq:box-product}, the conditional measure on a fixed
history full unstable plaque projects to $\mu_U$.
On common refinements with subordinate partitions, uniqueness
of disintegration identifies these conditionals up to restriction
and normalization, which preserve almost-everywhere local dimensions.
Thus $\mu_U$, and hence $\mu$, is exact dimensional of dimension
$\delta_u$. The same identification on fast plaques gives
conditional dimension $\delta_f$, proving (i) and (ii).

\smallskip

For (iii), fix a typical history $s$ and set
$\nu:=\mu_U$ and $\zeta:=(p_s)_*\nu$.
On a common local domain, the transverse coordinate constructed in
\cite[Section 6.4, Proposition 6.12]{QianXie2008}
and $p_s$ have the same fibers,
namely the local fast plaques.
The bi-Lipschitz leaf coordinates constructed there and the flow boxes
of Proposition \ref{prop:holomorphic-leaves} induce locally bi-Lipschitz
changes of transverse coordinates on countably many pieces with
fixed return time and inverse branch.
These constants may depend on the piece, since each fixed bi-Lipschitz
change preserves lower and upper local dimensions.

Within the fixed history full unstable plaque, refine these pieces
with the subordinate partitions and make them disjoint.
The pushforwards under $p_s$ of the restrictions of $\nu$ to these
pieces sum to $\zeta$.
After identifying the transverse coordinates by the preceding
bi-Lipschitz changes, each such measure is absolutely continuous
with respect to both $\zeta$ and the corresponding unrestricted transverse measure.
The Lebesgue differentiation theorem for finite Borel measures identifies their
lower and upper local dimensions almost everywhere with respect to
each restricted measure.
The transverse dimensions in \cite[Definitions 4.9--4.10]{QianXie2008}
are lower local dimensions. Proposition 4.12 there, applied with $i=2$,
therefore gives, for each $0<b<1$, 
$$\underline d_\zeta (v)\ge
\frac{(1-b)(2L-h_1-b)}{\lambda_2+b}
\qquad
\text{for $\zeta$-almost every $v$.}
$$
Taking a countable sequence $b\to0$ yields
$\underline d_\zeta\ge(2L-h_1)/\lambda_2$.
By (i), $\nu$ is exact dimensional of dimension $\delta_u$;
by (ii), its conditional measures along the fibers of $p_s$
are exact dimensional of dimension $\delta_f$.
Applying Lemma \ref{lem:conditional-mass} (i) in the local product
coordinates of Proposition \ref{prop:holomorphic-leaves} gives the reverse inequality
$\overline d_\zeta\le\delta_u-\delta_f=(2L-h_1)/\lambda_2$.
This proves (iii).

\smallskip

Subtracting $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{P}}(F)$ from the dimension formula in (i)
gives the desired identity.
Dupont's lower bound \cite[Corollary A]{Dupont2011} and
$\lambda_1>\lambda_2$ imply $h_1\le L$, while $h_1\ge0$
follows from non-negativity of conditional entropy.

label: prop:non-atomic
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:non-atomic}\label{prop:topological-ni}
Under \hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)}, if the fast direction is
history-dependent, then $\eta_x$ is non-atomic for
$\mu$-almost every $x$.
Moreover, for every measurable subset $E$ of a history box
with $\hat\mu(E)>0$ and every $\delta>0$, there are histories
$\Theta(x,s),\Theta(x,t)\in E$ over the same point $x$ such that
$0<\angle(E^f(\Theta(x,s)),E^f(\Theta(x,t)))<\delta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first establish an atomicity dichotomy. The remaining two steps
use standard arguments to exclude the Dirac case under history
dependence and to select the required pair of histories.

\smallskip

\emph{Step 1: Atomicity dichotomy.}
We show that either $\eta_x$ is Dirac for $\mu$-almost every $x$,
or $\eta_x$ is non-atomic for $\mu$-almost every $x$.

Set $A_x:=\mathbb P(DF_x)$.
Since $DF$ is non-singular on $K$, each $A_x$ is a projective
automorphism.
The equal weights of the inverse branches and equivariance
of the fast direction give
$$
 \eta_y=\frac1q\sum_{Fx=y}(A_x)_*\eta_x,
$$
where the sum runs over the $q$ preimages of $y$ in $K$.
Let $m(x)$ be the largest atom mass of $\eta_x$, with
$m(x)=0$ when $\eta_x$ is non-atomic, and define the transfer
operator 
on bounded measurable functions
by
$$
 (P\varphi)(y):=\frac1q\sum_{Fx=y}\varphi(x).
$$
The preceding identity gives $m\le Pm$.
Since $\int P\varphi\,d\mu=\int\varphi\,d\mu$,
we have $m=Pm$ almost everywhere.
Jensen's inequality gives $(Pm)^2\le P(m^2)$, and these
two functions have the same integral.
Equality therefore holds almost everywhere, so the values
of $m$ agree on the preimages of almost every $y$.
Their common value is $(Pm)(y)=m(y)$.
Thus $m(x)=m(Fx)$ almost everywhere, and ergodicity makes
$m$ constant almost everywhere. If this constant is zero, then $\eta_x$
is non-atomic almost everywhere.

Suppose instead
that $m>0$, and let $\mathcal A_x$ be the
set of atoms of $\eta_x$ having mass $m$.
For $\ell\in\mathcal A_y$, the identity
$$
 m=\frac1q\sum_{Fx=y}\eta_x(\{A_x^{-1}\ell\})
$$
forces every summand to equal $m$.
Hence $A_x^{-1}\mathcal A_{Fx}\subseteq\mathcal A_x$
almost everywhere
and therefore,
 for almost every $x$ and every $n\geq1$, we have
$\mathcal A_{F^n x}
 \subset \mathbb P(DF_x^n)\mathcal A_x$.
The support of $\eta_x$ consists of fast directions arising from
inverse histories over $x$. By \eqref{eq:uniform-domination} and compactness these
directions are uniformly transverse to $E^s(x)$.
Fix $\ell_x\in\mathcal A_x$.
In the splitting $\ell_x\oplus E^s(x)$, the other lines
of $\mathcal A_x$ have uniformly bounded slopes,
which contract under the projective action by
\eqref{eq:uniform-domination}.
Consequently, we have
$\operatorname{diam}
 \bigl(\mathbb P(DF_x^n)\mathcal A_x\bigr)
 \le C_0\tau^n$,
for some $C_0$ independent of $x$ and $n$.
Thus, setting $D(x):=\operatorname{diam}\mathcal A_x$, we have
$$
 \int D\,d\mu=\int D\circ F^n\,d\mu\le C_0\tau^n.
$$
Letting $n\to\infty$ gives $D=0$ almost everywhere.
Thus $\mathcal A_x=\{\ell(x)\}$ for a measurable line field
satisfying $A_x\ell(x)=\ell(Fx)$ almost everywhere.
The event $\{E^f(\hat x)=\ell(x_0)\}$ is invariant and has measure
$m>0$.
By ergodicity,
its $\hat\mu$-measure is therefore one,
so
$\eta_x$ is Dirac almost everywhere. This proves the dichotomy.







\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 2: Excluding the Dirac case.}
Suppose two inverse histories over a point $x$ have distinct
fast directions.
Continuity of the fast bundle gives a neighborhood $O$ of
$x$ in $K$ and two past cylinders $S_1,S_2\subset\Sigma^-$
such that the directions associated with $S_1$ and $S_2$
remain separated over every point of $O$.
The measures $\mu$ and $\beta$ have full support on $K$
and $\Sigma^-$, respectively.
Thus $\mu(O)>0$ and $\beta(S_1),\beta(S_2)>0$, so $\eta_y$
is non-Dirac for every $y\in O$.
This excludes the Dirac alternative and proves
non-atomicity under history dependence.

\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 3: Selection inside a positive measure set.}
Let $E\subset\Theta((K\cap U)\times S)$ have positive
$\hat\mu$-measure, and fix $\delta>0$.
By \eqref{eq:box-product} and Fubini's theorem, there is
$x\in K\cap U$ such that
$
E_x:=\{s\in S:\Theta(x,s)\in E\}
$
has positive $\beta$-measure and $\eta_x$ is non-atomic.
The pushforward of $\beta|_{E_x}/\beta(E_x)$ under
$s\mapsto E^f(\Theta(x,s))$ is absolutely continuous
with respect to $\eta_x$, and is therefore non-atomic.
Cover $\mathbb P(T_x\mathbb P^2)$ by finitely many sets of
angular diameter less than $\delta$.
One of these sets has positive mass for this pushforward,
and non-atomicity gives two histories $s,t\in E_x$
whose directions in that set are distinct.
Their angle lies strictly between $0$ and $\delta$,
as required.

label: prop:spreading
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:spreading}
Under \hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)},
if $h_1>0$,
 for every $\epsilon>0$ there is an integer
$\ell\ge1$ such that, for $\hat\mu$-almost every $\hat x$
and $\mathcal L^2$-almost every $h\in[0,1)^2$,
\eqref{eq:spreading-definition} holds at $x_0$, with $1/2$
replaced by $1/4$,
for all
sufficiently large $n$.
Moreover, there are a measurable set
$\mathcal G\subset\hat K\times[0,1)^2$ with
$(\hat\mu\otimes\mathcal L^2)(\mathcal G)>0$
and an integer $n_0$ such that the same conclusion holds
for every $(\hat x,h)\in\mathcal G$ and every $n\ge n_0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to consider $0<\epsilon<1$.
By Proposition \ref{prop:dimension}, almost every fast leaf
conditional is exact dimensional of dimension
$h_1/\lambda_1>0$, and is therefore non-atomic.

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 1: Transport of leaf masses and geometric distortion.}
We first establish the analogue of the invariance property in
\cite[Lemma 4.10]{LiPanTongXu2026}, using the full branch
Bernoulli coding.
Write $x_n:=\pi_0(\hat F^n\hat x)$, and let
$g_{\hat x,n}$ be the inverse branch from $x_n$ to $x_0$.
If $A\subset A_0$ are Borel subsets of the fast plaque
through $x_n$, and their images lie in the corresponding
plaque through $x_0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:leaf-mass-ratio}
 \frac{\nu_{\hat x}(g_{\hat x,n}A)}
      {\nu_{\hat x}(g_{\hat x,n}A_0)}
 =
 \frac{\nu_{\hat F^n\hat x}(A)}
      {\nu_{\hat F^n\hat x}(A_0)}
\end{equation}
whenever the denominators are positive.
Indeed, the Bernoulli property gives the cylinder identity
$
 (F^n)_*(q^n\mu|_{g_a(K)})=\mu
$
for every inverse word $a$ of length $n$, as established in
Section \ref{subsec:geometry}.
On compatible history boxes, this identity and
\eqref{eq:box-product}, followed by uniqueness of disintegration,
identify the corresponding leaf conditionals up to restriction
and multiplication by a positive scalar, which cancels in
the ratio.

We also need geometric control of the inverse branches.
Set
$$
 S_n(\hat x):=
 \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}
 \log\|DF_{x_j}|_{E^f(\hat F^j\hat x)}\|.
$$
The uniform margins of the chosen boxes and contraction
of the inverse branches allow us to choose $r_0>0$
such that each leaf disk $B_f(x_n,2r_0)$ lies in its
larger plaque and its inverse image lies in the
corresponding source coordinate neighborhood.
The restriction of $g_{\hat x,n}$ to this disk is univalent.
Koebe distortion on the smaller disks, together with the
uniform chart bounds in
Proposition \ref{prop:holomorphic-leaves}, gives a constant
$K_0\ge1$ such that
$$
 B_f(x_0,K_0^{-1}e^{-S_n}r)
 \subset g_{\hat x,n}(B_f(x_n,r))
 \subset B_f(x_0,K_0e^{-S_n}r)
 \quad \text{for every } 0<r\le r_0.
$$
The chart bounds absorb the comparison between the affine
norm and the leaf coordinates.
Shrink $r_0$ so that $K_0r_0\le1$.

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 2: Ball spreading at most scales.}
We now obtain the counterpart of the ball spreading conclusion in
\cite[Proposition 4.12]{LiPanTongXu2026}.
In \cite[Lemmas 4.14--4.15]{LiPanTongXu2026}, the mass drop is
first obtained for elements of a subordinate partition. Here the
non-atomicity of the fast leaf conditionals allows us to obtain
the required fixed scale mass drop directly for balls.

Fix a small $\rho>0$.
For $\hat\mu$-almost every $\hat y$, the point
$y_0$ belongs to the support of $\nu_{\hat y}$. Since
$\nu_{\hat y}$ is non-atomic, we have
$$
\frac{\nu_{\hat y}(B_f(y_0,r))}{\nu_{\hat y}(B_f(y_0,r_0))}
\to 0
\qquad\text{as }r\to0.
$$
Thus there are $0<r_1<r_0$ and a measurable set
$H\subset\hat K$ with $\hat\mu(H)>1-\rho$ such that, for every $\hat y\in H$, we have
$$
 \nu_{\hat y}(B_f(y_0,r_1))
 \le \frac14\nu_{\hat y}(B_f(y_0,r_0)).
$$
By ergodicity of $\hat\mu$ and Birkhoff's theorem, for almost
every orbit the asymptotic frequency of visits outside $H$ equals
$1-\hat\mu(H)<\rho$.

We now pass from return times to geometric scales as in the
proof of \cite[Proposition 4.12]{LiPanTongXu2026},
using the
distortion estimate from Step 1 in place of the comparison with
subordinate partition elements.
Uniform expansion and compactness give constants
$0<a\le b<\infty$ such that
$
 a\le S_{n+1}-S_n\le b$
 for every $\hat x\in\hat K$ and every $n\geq0$.
For $k\ge1$, set
$$
 n(k):=\min\{n\ge1:S_n\ge k\log2\}.
$$
Then we have
$$
 k\log2\le S_{n(k)}<k\log2+b
 \qquad \text{and} \qquad
 \frac{n(k)}k\to \frac{\log2}{\lambda_1}
$$
for $\hat\mu$-almost every $\hat x$.
Choose an integer $\ell_0\ge1$ such that
$2^{-\ell_0}\le K_0^{-1}r_1e^{-b}$.
If $\hat F^{n(k)}\hat x\in H$, the distortion estimates give
$
B_f(x_0,2^{-k-\ell_0})
\subset
g_{\hat x,n(k)}(B_f(x_{n(k)},r_1))
$
and
$g_{\hat x,n(k)}(B_f(x_{n(k)},r_0))
\subset B_f(x_0,2^{-k}).
$
Together with \eqref{eq:leaf-mass-ratio}, these inclusions yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ball-spreading}
 \nu_{\hat x}(B_f(x_0,2^{-k-\ell_0}))
 \le \frac14\nu_{\hat x}(B_f(x_0,2^{-k})).
\end{equation}
Each integer occurs as $n(k)$ for at most
$M:=\lceil b/\log2\rceil+1$ values of $k$.
For each integer $J\ge1$, the number of scales $1\le k\le J$ for which
$\hat F^{n(k)}\hat x\notin H$ is at most $M$ times the number
of visits outside $H$ at times $1,\ldots,n(J)$.
The preceding visit frequency
bound and the limit for $n(J)/J$ show that
the upper density of scales failing
\eqref{eq:ball-spreading} is at most
$
M\rho\frac{\log2}{\lambda_1}$.
Choose $\rho$ so that this quantity is less than $\epsilon/4$.

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 3: From balls to planar dyadic squares.}
We now adapt the boundary frequency argument of
\cite[Lemma 4.16]{LiPanTongXu2026} from intervals in $\mathbb R$
to squares in $\mathbb R^2$.
For a fixed leaf point $x$ in leaf coordinates, the condition
that $x$ lies within $2^{-j-q_0}$ of the boundary of
$\mathcal D_j^h(x)$ is equivalent to
$2^j(x-h)\bmod\mathbb Z^2$ lying in a boundary strip
in $\mathbb T^2$ of Lebesgue measure $O(2^{-q_0})$.
Ergodicity of the doubling map on $\mathbb T^2$ implies that,
for $\mathcal L^2$-almost every $h\in[0,1)^2$, these boundary
scales have frequency $O(2^{-q_0})$.
Choose an integer $q_0$ so that this frequency is less than
$\epsilon/4$.

At every scale $j$ for which
$
\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\mathcal D_j^h(x))
\ge2^{-j-q_0},
$
we have
$$
 B_f(x,2^{-j-q_0})\subset\mathcal D_j^h(x)
 \qquad \text{and}\qquad
 \mathcal D_{j+\ell}^h(x)
 \subset B_f(x,2^{-j-\ell+1}).
$$
Set $\ell:=q_0+\ell_0+1$.
Applying \eqref{eq:ball-spreading} at $k=j+q_0$ gives
$$
 \nu_{\hat x}(\mathcal D_{j+\ell}^h(x))
 \le\frac14\nu_{\hat x}(\mathcal D_j^h(x))
$$
whenever both
$\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\mathcal D_j^h(x))\ge2^{-j-q_0}$ and
\eqref{eq:ball-spreading} at $k=j+q_0$ hold.
The exceptional scales have upper density less than
$\epsilon/2$.
After absorbing the finitely many initial and terminal
scales, this proves \eqref{eq:spreading-definition} at $x_0$,
with $1/2$ replaced by $1/4$,
for all sufficiently large $n$.

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 4: Conclusion.}
Fubini's theorem gives the assertion for
$\hat\mu\otimes\mathcal L^2$-almost every $(\hat x,h)$.
Finally, let $\mathcal G_N$ be the set of pairs for which
\eqref{eq:spreading-definition},
with $1/2$ replaced by $1/4$,
holds for every $n\ge N$.
These measurable sets increase to a set of full product
measure, so some $\mathcal G_{n_0}$ has positive measure.
Taking $\mathcal G:=\mathcal G_{n_0}$ proves the uniformity
assertion.

label: lem:local-model
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:local-model}
Assume that 
\hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)} holds, the fast direction is history-dependent,
$\gamma_f>0$, and $0<\gamma_t<1$.
Fix $\kappa>0$ with $\gamma_t<1-2\kappa$, and let $\ell$
be given by Proposition \ref{prop:spreading} with error
$\kappa/1000$.
For every $0<\epsilon<1/256$, there is an integer $N$,
depending only on the history box, $\kappa,\ell$, and
$\epsilon$, such that for arbitrarily large integers
$k\ge N$ there are two histories $i,j$ through a common
point, a translation $\mathbf h$, an $i$-leaf square
$Q_0$ corresponding to $Q_f\in\mathcal D_{6k}^{h_f}$, 
and measurable sets
$G\subset G'\subset K\cap U$ such that the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item
The fast directions at the common point make an angle
comparable to $2^{-k}$.
In $i$-coordinates centered at some $z_*\in G\cap Q_0$,
with $Q_0\subset\{v=0\}$, an affine normalization of
$p_j$ gives \eqref{eq:projection-sum-model} with
$|c|\asymp2^{-k}$ and uniform constants.

\item
Let $\nu_{i,Q_0}$ denote the normalized $i$-leaf conditional
on $Q_0$.
Then $\nu_{i,Q_0}(G)>1/2$.
At every point of $G\cap Q_0$, at most $\kappa k/20$
starting scales in $[6k,7k-\ell]$ fail the mass inequality
appearing in
\eqref{eq:spreading-definition}.

\item
On $G'$, the spatial ball
estimate in
Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (i), and, for $s=i,j$,
the transverse ball
estimate in Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (ii),
hold with error $\epsilon$ for every $0<r<2^{-N}$.
The product partition
estimate in Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (iii)
holds with $s=i$ for every $n\geq N$.

\item Every $z\in G$ satisfies
$\nu(B(z,r)\setminus G')
 \leq2\epsilon\,\nu(B(z,r))$
for every $0<r<2^{-N}$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
The counterpart of (P1) in
\cite[Section 6.2]{LiPanTongXu2026}
is given by Proposition \ref{prop:spreading}.
The counterparts of (P2)--(P4) are the spatial,
transverse, and product partition estimates of
Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (i), (ii), and (iii),
respectively.
In Step 2, we establish the counterparts of (P5)--(P6)
by applying the Lebesgue differentiation theorem for
finite Borel measures on Euclidean space twice,
with respect to the spatial measure $\nu$.
Step 3 selects two histories whose fast directions are close and
distinct, constructs the nested sets $G\subset G'$, and proves (iv).
Step 4 selects the leaf square $Q_0$ and proves (ii). Step 5
recenters the coordinates and normalizes $p_j$, completing the proof
of (i), and transfers the mass estimates to the normalized
coordinates, proving (iii).


\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 1: Uniform spreading and mass estimates.}
In \cite[Section 6.2]{LiPanTongXu2026}, the good sets
are chosen with measure sufficiently close to one so that
a history section satisfies the large measure hypothesis
of \cite[Proposition 3.5]{LiPanTongXu2026}. 
Here Proposition \ref{prop:non-atomic} applies to every
positive measure subset of the history box.

After discarding a $\beta_S$-null subset of $S$, we may assume
that, for every remaining history $s$, the conditional measure on
the corresponding full unstable plaque projects to $\nu$.
Moreover, the fast leaf conditionals of $\nu$ relative to the
$s$-foliation are exact dimensional of dimension $\gamma_f$, and
$\zeta_s$ is exact dimensional of dimension $\gamma_t$, as in
Proposition \ref{prop:dimension}.
By Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles},
applied
with error $\epsilon/2$, 
the estimates in items (i)--(iii) of that lemma
hold
almost everywhere in the product box.
We use the fixed charts $(u_s,v_s)$ in the spreading
argument of Proposition \ref{prop:spreading}.
Disintegrating $\hat\mu$ along the fast plaques and using Fubini's theorem, the
conclusion of Proposition \ref{prop:spreading} holds at almost every
point with respect to almost every local fast leaf conditional and for
$\mathcal L^2$-almost every translation $h_f$. 
The leaf conditionals of $\nu$
are normalized restrictions of these measures.
L\'evy's upward theorem \cite[Section 14.2]{Williams1991},
applied to the nested leaf dyadic partitions, implies that,
at almost every point
of the restricting set, its relative conditional mass
in the containing dyadic square tends to one.
Consequently, at all sufficiently small scales, the restricting
set occupies at least half of the conditional mass of the parent
dyadic square. Proposition \ref{prop:spreading} therefore gives
the required factor $1/2$ after restriction.
For almost every triple, the number of failing starts
at depth $7k$ is therefore at most
$7\kappa k/1000+O(1)$, where the finite error may depend
on the triple.
For all sufficiently large $k$, at most $\kappa k/20$
starts in $[6k,7k-\ell]$ fail.
Choose an integer $N$ and a positive measure set
$\mathcal G_2\subset(K\cap U)\times S\times[0,1)^4$
on which this spreading count holds for every $k\ge N$,
the product partition estimate
in Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (iii)
holds for every $n\ge N$, and
the 
spatial and transverse
ball estimates
in Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (i)--(ii)
hold for every $0<r<2^{-N}$.
Such a choice is possible since the sets on which
these conclusions hold increase to a set of full
product measure as $N\to\infty$.

After restricting $\mathcal G_2$ to a subset of positive
measure, we may also assume that its spatial coordinates
have a fixed positive distance from $\partial U$.
Increase $N$ so that the small balls and coordinate cubes
used in the construction remain inside $U$.
This gives the counterparts of (P1)--(P4) in \cite{LiPanTongXu2026} with the
same integer $N$ at every point of $\mathcal G_2$.

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 2: Two density refinements.}
We now establish the two density properties corresponding
to (P5)--(P6) in \cite[Section 6.2]{LiPanTongXu2026}.
The first refinement will ensure that the final set $G'$ has large
density around every point of $G$, while the second refinement will ensure that
$G$ has large density around the common point selected in Step 3.

For a measurable set $\mathcal E$ in the product box,
write
$\mathcal E(s,\mathbf h):=
\{z:(z,s,\mathbf h)\in\mathcal E\}$
for its spatial section.
For almost every $(s,\mathbf h)$, the Lebesgue
differentiation theorem applied to
$\mathbf 1_{\mathcal G_2(s,\mathbf h)}$ with respect
to $\nu$ gives
\[
 \frac{\nu(B(z,r)\cap\mathcal G_2(s,\mathbf h))}
      {\nu(B(z,r))}
 \to1
 \qquad\text{as }r\to0
\]
for $\nu$-almost every $z\in\mathcal G_2(s,\mathbf h)$.
By Fubini's theorem, this holds for almost every
$(z,s,\mathbf h)\in\mathcal G_2$.
Increase $N$ and choose a positive measure subset
$\mathcal G_3\subset\mathcal G_2$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:density-P5}
\nu(B(z,r)\setminus\mathcal G_2(s,\mathbf h))
 \le\epsilon\nu(B(z,r))\quad
 \text{ for every } 0<r<2^{-N}
\end{equation}
at every $(z,s,\mathbf h)\in\mathcal G_3$.
This is the counterpart of (P5) of \cite{LiPanTongXu2026}.

Apply the Lebesgue differentiation theorem to the spatial
sections of $\mathcal G_3$.
After increasing $N$, choose a positive measure subset
$\mathcal G_4\subset\mathcal G_3$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:density-P6}
 \nu(B(z,r)\setminus\mathcal G_3(s,\mathbf h))
 \le\epsilon\nu(B(z,r))
 \quad \text{ for every } 0<r<2^{-N}
\end{equation}
at every $(z,s,\mathbf h)\in\mathcal G_4$.
This gives the counterpart of (P6) of \cite{LiPanTongXu2026}.
All earlier estimates remain valid after increasing $N$.

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 3: Selection of histories with close directions.}
With $N$ fixed, Fubini's theorem gives a translation $\mathbf h$
such that the set
$\{(z,s):(z,s,\mathbf h)\in\mathcal G_4\}$
has positive $\nu\otimes\beta_S$-measure.
By \eqref{eq:box-product}, this corresponds to
a positive
$\hat\mu$-measure subset of the history box.
Proposition \ref{prop:non-atomic} therefore gives, for arbitrarily
large $k\ge N$, two histories $i,j$ over a common point $x$,
with $(x,i,\mathbf h),(x,j,\mathbf h)\in\mathcal G_4$,
whose fast directions make an angle $\theta$ satisfying
$2^{-k-1}<\theta\le2^{-k}$.
Set
\[
 G:=\mathcal G_3(i,\mathbf h)\cap\mathcal G_3(j,\mathbf h)
 \qquad
 \text{and}
 \qquad
 G':=\mathcal G_2(i,\mathbf h)\cap\mathcal G_2(j,\mathbf h).
\]
Applying \eqref{eq:density-P6} to both histories gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:G-density}
 \nu(B(x,r)\setminus G)\le2\epsilon\nu(B(x,r))
 \quad \text{for every}
 \quad 0<r<2^{-N}.
\end{equation}
Similarly, \eqref{eq:density-P5} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Gprime-density}
 \nu(B(z,r)\setminus G')\le2\epsilon\nu(B(z,r))
 \quad \text{for every} \quad
 z\in G \quad \text{and} \quad 0<r<2^{-N}.
\end{equation}
Before recentering and normalization, the estimates in
Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (i)--(iii), with error
$\epsilon/2$, and the spreading estimates hold on $G'$ for both
histories. Estimate \eqref{eq:G-density} is used to select the leaf
square $Q_0$, while \eqref{eq:Gprime-density} proves (iv).

The uniform $C^2$ chart bounds give a uniform Lipschitz
bound for the fast directions as functions of the spatial
point with history fixed.
Their variation on $B(x,2^{-2k})$ is therefore
$O(2^{-2k})=o(2^{-k})$.
Hence the angle between the two directions remains
comparable to $2^{-k}$ throughout this ball.

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 4: Selection of a leaf square.}
We follow the doubling and density transfer argument
of \cite[Lemmas 6.5--6.6 and Proposition 6.9]
{LiPanTongXu2026}.
Since $D\le4$,
the two-sided spatial ball estimate in
Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (i) yields
a scale
at which the doubling ratio is less than $32$.
Indeed, there is an integer $q$ with $2k<q\le4k$ such that,
for $r=2^{-q}$, one has
$\nu(B(x,2r))/\nu(B(x,r))<32$.
Otherwise, multiplying the successive ratios would give
$\nu(B(x,2^{-2k}))/\nu(B(x,2^{-4k}))\ge2^{10k}$.
On the other hand, applying the upper spatial ball bound at radius
$2^{-2k}$ and the lower bound at radius $2^{-4k}$ gives
\[
 \frac{\nu(B(x,2^{-2k}))}{\nu(B(x,2^{-4k}))}
 \leq 2^{(2D+6\epsilon)k}<2^{10k},
\]
since $D\leq4$ and $\epsilon<1/256$.


Consider the cubes of the fixed $i$-coordinate product
grid at level $6k$ meeting $B(x,r)$.
Their diameters are $O(2^{-6k})=o(r)$, so their union
contains $B(x,r)$ and is contained in $B(x,2r)$
for large $k$.
Estimate \eqref{eq:G-density} and the doubling estimate
show that the mass outside $G$ is at most $64\epsilon$
times the mass of this union.
Thus some cube $Q$ of positive mass satisfies
$\nu(Q\setminus G)\le64\epsilon\nu(Q)$.
Since $64\epsilon<1/4$, disintegration along the
$i$-leaves gives an $i$-leaf square $Q_0$ whose
normalized conditional assigns mass greater than
$1/2$ to $G$.
Choose this square on a leaf where the conditional
measures and spreading estimates are defined.
Its leaf coordinate has side length $2^{-6k}$,
and Step 1 provides the spreading count at every
point of $G\cap Q_0$.
This proves (ii).

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 5: Recentering and normalization.}
Choose $z_*\in G\cap Q_0$ and center the $i$-coordinates
at $z_*$, so that $Q_0\subset\{v=0\}$.
Since $Q_0\subset B(x,2r)\subset B(x,2^{-2k})$,
the angle between the fast directions determined by histories $i,j$
at $z_*$ is still comparable to $2^{-k}$.
The affine normalization of $p_j$ and Taylor expansion
at $z_*$ give \eqref{eq:projection-sum-model} with
$|c|\asymp2^{-k}$ and uniform constants.
This proves (i).

Translate the dyadic grids by the same coordinate shifts,
and continue to write $\mathbf h$ for their translation parameters.
The leaf
squares and the elements of the product partitions are unchanged
as subsets of $U$, so the spreading ratios remain valid and the
estimate in Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (iii) remains
valid with $s=i$. The spatial ball estimate in
Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (i)
is unchanged.
The affine normalization of $p_j$ changes transverse
radii by uniformly bounded factors.
The $\epsilon/2$ margin in the original ball estimates
therefore gives the transverse ball estimates in
Lemma \ref{prop:rectangles} (ii)
with error $\epsilon$,
for $s=i,j$, after increasing $N$.
Since the normalization factors are uniformly bounded, the required
increase of $N$ depends only on the uniform chart bounds and
$\epsilon$, and not on the selected histories or on $k$. Thus $N$
may be chosen with this additional property already in Step 1.
This proves (iii).

label: thm:discrete-growth
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:discrete-growth}
Fix two integers $m,\ell\ge1$ and two real numbers $0<\kappa<1$ and $R_*\ge1$.
There exists $\delta>0$ such that, for all sufficiently
large $n$, the following holds.
Suppose that $\omega$ is a $2^{-n}$-grid probability
and that $A,B\subset[-R_*,R_*]^m$ lie on the same grid.
Assume that $(\omega,A)$ is $(n,\ell,\kappa)$-spreading and that
$1\le |B|\le 2^{(1-\kappa)n}$. For each $a\in A$, let
$B_a\subseteq B$ 
be a subset
such that
$|B_a|\ge |B|^{1-\delta}$.
Set $\Sigma:=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B_a\}$. Then the
following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item
We have $|\Sigma|\ge|B|^{1+\delta}$.
\item
For every $C_0\ge0$, if $Z\subset\mathbb R^m$ has the property
that, for every $a\in A$ and $b\in B_a$, there exists
$z\in Z$ with $|a+b-z|\le C_0 2^{-n}$, then
$N_{2^{-n}}(Z)\ge c(m,C_0)|B|^{1+\delta}$.
\end{enumerate}

label: lem:discrete-model
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:discrete-model}
Let $i,j,\mathbf h,Q_0,k$, and $G\subset G'$ be given by
Lemma \ref{lem:local-model}, 
and use the centered $i$-coordinates and
normalized projection $p_j$ from Lemma \ref{lem:local-model} (i).
There are constants $C,R_*\ge1$, independent of
$\epsilon$ and $k$, such that for all sufficiently
large $k$ one can construct a $2^{-k}$-grid
probability $\omega$, sets $A,B\subset[-R_*,R_*]^2$
on the same grid, subsets $B_\xi\subset B$ for
$\xi\in A$, and a 
set $\mathcal R\subset G'$
satisfying the following:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item
$(\omega,A)$ is $(k,\ell,\kappa)$-spreading
in the sense of \eqref{eq:grid-spreading};
\item
$|B|\le2^{k(\gamma_t+C\epsilon)}$,
$|B_\xi|\ge2^{k(\gamma_t-C\epsilon)}$ for every
$\xi\in A$, and
$N_{r_2}(p_j(\mathcal R))\le2^{k(\gamma_t+C\epsilon)}$;
\item
Every sum $\xi+b$, with $\xi\in A$ and $b\in B_\xi$,
lies within $O(2^{-k})$ of a point of
$p_j(\mathcal R)/(cr_0)$, with a uniform implicit constant.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: Discretization and spreading of the leaf conditional.}
In \cite[Sections 6.4--6.5]{LiPanTongXu2026},
the leaf conditional is normalized on an interval,
and Claim 2 there
verifies its spreading property after rescaling.
Here we normalize on the leaf square $Q_0$ and assign
its descendant masses to a planar grid.

Use the normalized leaf conditional $\nu_{i,Q_0}$
from Lemma \ref{lem:local-model} (ii).
Since $Q_0$ lies at ambient dyadic level $6k$, each of its
descendants at level $7k$
(that is, after $k$ dyadic refinements of $Q_0$)
has a $u$-coordinate square of the form
$a+[0,r_1)^2\subset\mathbb R^2\simeq\mathbb C$.
Assign its $\nu_{i,Q_0}$-mass to the grid point $a/r_0$.
Since $r_1/r_0=2^{-k}$, these representatives lie on a
translated $2^{-k}$ lattice.
This defines $\omega$.
We equip the lattice with the dyadic partitions
obtained by rescaling the original leaf grid by
$r_0^{-1}$.
Let $A$ consist of the representatives whose descendants
carry positive $\nu_{i,Q_0}$-mass from $G$.
Then $\omega(A)>1/2$.
For each $\xi\in A$, choose $z_\xi=(u_\xi,0)$
in that descendant and in $G$, so that
$\xi=u_\xi/r_0+O(2^{-k})$.

This discretization preserves the dyadic mass ratios
needed to verify \eqref{eq:grid-spreading}.
Restriction to the parent square $Q_0$ cancels in
every descendant ratio, and the rescaled levels $0,1,\ldots,k$
correspond to the original levels $6k, 6k+1,\ldots,7k$.
The representative and $z_\xi$ belong to corresponding
ancestors through depth $k$.
Lemma \ref{lem:local-model} (ii) leaves at most
$\kappa k/20$ failing starts.
There are $k-\ell+1$ possible starts, and
$\ell-1\le\kappa k/20$ for large $k$.
Thus at least $(1-\kappa/10)k$ starts satisfy the
required mass inequality, proving (i).

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 2: Transverse sets and their lower bounds.}
The construction of the transverse sets in
\cite[Lemma 6.10]{LiPanTongXu2026} combines
the spatial mass bound (P2), the density property (P5),
and the product partition bound (P4).
We use the spatial ball and product partition estimates in
Lemma \ref{lem:local-model} (iii), together with the density
estimate in Lemma \ref{lem:local-model} (iv),
to select a
nearby cube $P_\xi$ and estimate the number of transverse grid
points arising from $P_\xi\cap G'$.

For each $\xi\in A$, 
combining Lemma
\ref{lem:local-model} (iv)
at $z_\xi$
with the lower bound for spatial balls in
Lemma \ref{lem:local-model} (iii) gives
$\nu(B(z_\xi,r_1)\cap G')
\ge(1-2\epsilon)r_1^{D+\epsilon}$.
Consider the product grid in the $i$-coordinates with side
$r_1=2^{-7k}$ in both the $u$- and $v$-coordinates. The ball
$B(z_\xi,r_1)$ meets only boundedly many elements of this grid.
Consequently, one such element $P_\xi$ satisfies
$\nu(P_\xi\cap G')\gtrsim r_1^{D+\epsilon}$
and $P_\xi\subset B(z_\xi,C'r_1)$, with $C'$ uniform.

Set $\mathcal R:=\bigcup_{\xi\in A}(P_\xi\cap G')$.
Round each point of $p_i(P_\xi\cap G')/(cr_0)$ to a nearest
point of the same translated $2^{-k}$-lattice as $A$, let
$B_\xi$ be the set of grid points obtained in this way, and set
$B:=\bigcup_{\xi\in A}B_\xi$.
Since $|c|r_0\asymp r_1$, we have
$r_2/(|c|r_0)\asymp r_2/r_1=2^{-k}$.
Thus $B_\xi$ records the discretized transverse positions
available near the leaf position $\xi$.
Moreover, $|u|=O(r_0)$ and $|v|=O(r_1)$ on $\mathcal R$, so all the
grid sets lie in a fixed box $[-R_*,R_*]^2$.

The points rounding to one $b\in B_\xi$ have
transverse coordinates in a set of diameter $O(r_2)$.
Inside $P_\xi$, these points meet only boundedly many
elements of $\mathcal R_{k,i}^{\mathbf h}$, since the
leaf side of $P_\xi$ is $r_1$.
Each contributing partition element contains a point of $G'$
and therefore has mass at most
$2^{-k(7\gamma_f+8\gamma_t-\epsilon)}$
by Lemma \ref{lem:local-model} (iii).
Summing over the rounded transverse positions gives
\[
 |B_\xi|
 \gtrsim
 \frac{\nu(P_\xi\cap G')}
      {2^{-k(7\gamma_f+8\gamma_t-\epsilon)}}
 \gtrsim 2^{k(\gamma_t-8\epsilon)},
\]
where we used $7\gamma_f+8\gamma_t-7D=\gamma_t$.
Absorbing the fixed constants for sufficiently large $k$
gives $|B_\xi|\ge2^{k(\gamma_t-C\epsilon)}$
with a uniform $C$.

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 3: Upper bounds for the transverse projections.}
In \cite[Section 6.3]{LiPanTongXu2026}, the upper
covering estimate follows by comparing transverse
masses at the size of the projected region and at
the covering scale, using (P3).
We make the same comparison for $\zeta_i$ and $\zeta_j$
at scales $r_1$ and $r_2$.

On $\mathcal R$, we have $|u|=O(r_0)$ and $|v|=O(r_1)$.
By \eqref{eq:projection-sum-model}, both
$p_i(\mathcal R)$ and $p_j(\mathcal R)$ lie in balls
of radius $O(r_1)$.
For $s=i,j$, take a maximal disjoint family of balls of
radius $r_2/2$ centered on $p_s(\mathcal R)$.
Every center is the projection of a point of $G'$,
so each ball has $\zeta_s$-mass bounded below by
a constant times $r_2^{\gamma_t+\epsilon}$.
The union of these balls is contained in
$B(p_s(z_0),Cr_1)$ for some $z_0\in \mathcal R\subset G'$, where $C$
is uniform. By Lemma \ref{lem:local-model} (iii), this ball has
$\zeta_s$-mass $O(r_1^{\gamma_t-\epsilon})$.
Comparing these masses and doubling the radii of
the disjoint balls yields
\[
 N_{r_2}(p_s(\mathcal R))
 \lesssim
 \frac{r_1^{\gamma_t-\epsilon}}
      {r_2^{\gamma_t+\epsilon}}
 =2^{k(\gamma_t+15\epsilon)}.
\]
After increasing $C$ and taking $k$ sufficiently large,
this is at most $2^{k(\gamma_t+C\epsilon)}$.
For $s=j$, this is the required covering bound.
For $s=i$, each transverse $r_2$-ball contributes
only a bounded number of rounded grid points,
giving the same upper bound for $|B|$.
This proves (ii).

\medskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 4: Approximation by restricted sums.}
In \cite[Section 6.5]{LiPanTongXu2026},
Lemma A.4 compares the second projection with
translated transverse sets, and Lemma A.6 gives
the geometric estimates used to apply Corollary 5.2.
Here \eqref{eq:projection-sum-model} directly gives
the approximation by $\xi+b$ after normalization.

If $b\in B_\xi$ is represented by
$(u,v)\in P_\xi\cap G'$, then
$b=v/(cr_0)+O(2^{-k})$ and
$|u-u_\xi|=O(r_1)$.
Dividing \eqref{eq:projection-sum-model} by $cr_0$
therefore gives
\[
 \frac{p_j(u,v)}{cr_0}
 =\xi+b+O(2^{-k}).
\]
The error from replacing $u$ by $u_\xi$ is
$O(r_1/r_0)=O(2^{-k})$, the rounding errors are
$O(2^{-k})$, and the normalized quadratic error is
$O(r_0^2/r_1)=O(2^{-5k})$.
Thus every allowed sum lies within $O(2^{-k})$
of a point of $p_j(\mathcal R)/(cr_0)$, proving (iii).

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $0<\gamma_t<1$;
Proposition \ref{prop:dimension} excludes $\gamma_t=0$.
Choose $\kappa>0$ with $\gamma_t<1-2\kappa<1-\kappa$,
and choose the spreading window $\ell$ from
Proposition \ref{prop:spreading} with error $\kappa/1000$.
Let $C,R_*$ be the constants 
given by
Lemma \ref{lem:discrete-model}.
Theorem \ref{thm:discrete-growth}, applied with $m=2$ and
parameters $\kappa,\ell,R_*$, gives a growth exponent
$\delta_*>0$.
Set $\delta:=\min\{\delta_*,1/2\}$.
The theorem remains valid with this exponent.
Choose $0<\epsilon<1/256$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),ref=\arabic*,leftmargin=*]
\item\label{cond:growth-cutoff}
$0<\gamma_t-C\epsilon$ and
$\gamma_t+C\epsilon<1-\kappa$;
\item\label{cond:growth-gap}
$(\gamma_t-C\epsilon)(1+\delta)>\gamma_t+C\epsilon$.
\end{enumerate}
These conditions hold for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$,
since $\gamma_t>0$ and $\delta>0$.
All parameters are fixed before selecting the histories
and $k$.

For arbitrarily large $k$, Lemmas \ref{lem:local-model}
and \ref{lem:discrete-model} provide
$\omega,A,B$, 
the family $(B_\xi)_{\xi\in A}$, and
$\mathcal R$.
Lemma \ref{lem:discrete-model} (i) gives the required spreading
property and, in particular, $A\ne\emptyset$. Choosing
$\xi\in A$, Lemma \ref{lem:discrete-model} (ii) and Condition (1)
give
$|B|\ge |B_\xi|
 \ge 2^{k(\gamma_t-C\epsilon)}>1$ and
 $|B|\le 2^{k(\gamma_t+C\epsilon)}
 \le 2^{(1-\kappa)k}$.
Condition \eqref{cond:growth-gap} gives
\[
 \frac{\gamma_t-C\epsilon}{\gamma_t+C\epsilon}
 >
 \frac{1}{1+\delta}>1-\delta.
\]
Hence Lemma \ref{lem:discrete-model} (ii) also gives
$|B_\xi|\ge |B|^{1-\delta}$ for every $\xi\in A$.
Apply Theorem \ref{thm:discrete-growth} with $n=k$
and $Z=p_j(\mathcal R)/(cr_0)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:discrete-model} (iii), $Z$
verifies the
approximation hypothesis of
Theorem \ref{thm:discrete-growth} (ii), and hence
$N_{2^{-k}}(Z)\ge c_0|B|^{1+\delta}$.
Multiplication by $cr_0$ takes $Z$ onto
$p_j(\mathcal R)$ and scales distances by $|c|r_0$.
Since $|c|r_0\,2^{-k}\asymp r_2$, comparison of
covering numbers at comparable radii gives
\[
 N_{r_2}(p_j(\mathcal R))
 \ge c_1|B|^{1+\delta}
 \ge c_1 2^{k(\gamma_t-C\epsilon)(1+\delta)}.
\]
Lemma \ref{lem:discrete-model} (ii) bounds the same
covering number by $2^{k(\gamma_t+C\epsilon)}$.
By \eqref{cond:growth-gap}, we have $(\gamma_t-C\epsilon)(1+\delta)>\gamma_t+C\epsilon$, which makes these inequalities
incompatible for large $k$.
Therefore $\gamma_t\ge1$.

label: rmk:threshold
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:threshold}
Although the transverse measures live on
$\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb R^2$, the restricted sum estimate in
Theorem \ref{thm:discrete-growth},
as in Wu's 
theorem,
forces growth only below cardinality exponent $1$. Under its
spreading hypothesis, this threshold is sharp: the spreading
measure may be supported on a line, along which the transverse set
may already be saturated at cardinality of order $2^n$. Forcing
growth beyond exponent $1$ would therefore require additional
genuinely two-dimensional non-concentration.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\gamma_f=0$, then $h_1=0$. If $\gamma_f>0$,
Proposition \ref{prop:local-growth} 
gives $\gamma_t\ge1$, and hence
$h_1=\lambda_1\gamma_f
 =2L-\lambda_2\gamma_t
 \le 2L-\lambda_2$.
Thus,
 $h_1\le\max\{0,2L-\lambda_2\}$.
For $\lambda_2>L$, this implies
$L-h_1\ge\min\{L,\lambda_2-L\}$, and the entropy defect identity
in Proposition \ref{prop:dimension} gives
$\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_F-\mathcal D_{\mathrm{P}}(F)\ge\min\{L,\lambda_2-L\}
(\lambda_2^{-1}-\lambda_1^{-1})>0$.

If $\lambda_2\ge2L$, the alternative $\gamma_f>0$ would give
$h_1\le2L-\lambda_2\le0$, so $h_1=0$ and
$\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_F=2L/\lambda_2$.
If $L<\lambda_2<2L$, the dimension formula in
Proposition \ref{prop:dimension} is decreasing in $h_1$, since
$\lambda_1>\lambda_2$. Substituting the maximal allowed value
$h_1=2L-\lambda_2$ gives
$\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_F\ge1+(2L-\lambda_2)/\lambda_1$,
which proves parts (i) and (ii).

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{cor:measurable-rigidity}
Assume \hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)}.
If $\lambda_1>\lambda_2>\log d$ and $\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_F=\mathcal D_{\mathrm{P}}(F)$, there is
a continuous complex line field $\ell$ on $K$ such that
$DF_x\ell(x)=\ell(Fx)$ for $x\in K$ and
$E^f(\hat x)=\ell(x_0)$ for $\hat x\in\hat K$.
Indeed, Theorem \ref{thm:mechanism} forces $E^f$ to be constant
on every fiber of $\hat K\to K$. This projection is a quotient map,
since it is a continuous surjection from a compact space to a
Hausdorff space, so the continuous fast bundle descends to $\ell$.
Its invariance follows from
that of $E^f$.

label: lem:quadratic-family
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:quadratic-family}
The four inverse branches 
of $F_{R,t}$
on $Q_R$
extend to a bounded convex complex neighborhood of $Q_R$ on which
they generate a full branch repeller $K_{R,t}$ supporting
$\mu_{F_{R,t}}$ and satisfying \hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)}.
Moreover, we have
$\lambda_1(R,t)=\lambda_p>\lambda_2(R,t)$ and
$
\log12<\lambda_2(R,t)<\log26.
$
The function $t\mapsto\lambda_2(R,t)$ is continuous, and
for $t\ne0$ the fast direction is history-dependent.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The four inverse branches of $F_{R,t}$ on $Q_R$ 
are
$g_{\sigma,\tau}$, $\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}$, given by
$$
g_{\sigma,\tau}(z,w)=(Z,W),\qquad
Z=\sigma\sqrt{R^2+z},\qquad
W=\tau\sqrt{100+w-tZ}.
$$
Let $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$ denote the operator
norms induced by the maximum and Euclidean vector norms,
respectively.
The parameter bounds give
$$
 R-1<|Z|<R+1, \qquad
 6<|W|<13, \qquad \text{and} \qquad
 \|Dg_{\sigma,\tau}\|_\infty<1/10.
$$
Their images are compactly contained in $Q_R$ and disjoint, 
and
$
 \|Dg_{\sigma,\tau}\|_2
 \le\sqrt2\|Dg_{\sigma,\tau}\|_\infty<1.
$
These properties persist on a small bounded convex complex
thickening of $Q_R$.
The leading homogeneous terms $(z^2,w^2)$ have no common zero
outside the origin, so $F_{R,t}$ extends to a degree two holomorphic
endomorphism of $\mathbb P^2$.
The four-branch coding identifies the Bernoulli measure
on its real repeller with $\mu_{F_{R,t}}$.

The vertical direction is invariant.
For a complementary line
$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}(1,s_t(\hat x))$, invariance gives
$$
 s_t(\hat x)
 =\frac{t}{2z_{-1}}
  +\frac{w_{-1}}{z_{-1}}s_t(\hat x^-),
 \qquad \hat x^-:=\hat F^{-1}\hat x.
$$
Since $|w/z|<13/(R-1)<1$, this graph transform contracts
and gives a dominated fast bundle with
$
 |s_t|\le M_t:=\frac{|t|}{2R-28}.
$
Its slope is real, since the transform preserves real slopes.
This proves that \hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)} holds.
By \cite{Jonsson1999}, the Lyapunov exponents are
$$
 \lambda_1(R,t)
 =\int\log|2z|\,d\mu_{F_{R,t}}=\lambda_p
 \qquad \text{and} \qquad
 \lambda_2(R,t)
 =\int\log|2w|\,d\mu_{F_{R,t}},
$$
since the $z$-projection of $\mu_{F_{R,t}}$ is $\mu_{p_R}$.
Thus
$
 \lambda_p>\log(2(R-1))>\log26>
 \lambda_2(R,t)>\log12.
$
The coding map varies continuously with $t$, uniformly over
the symbolic space, while the Bernoulli measure is fixed.
Since $|w|>6$, the integral defining $\lambda_2(R,t)$
is therefore continuous.

It remains to prove history dependence when $t\ne0$.
The bound
$
|2w_{-1}s_t(\hat x^-)|\le26M_t<|t|/2
$
shows that $s_t(\hat x)$ has the sign of $t/z_{-1}$
and absolute value greater than $|t|/[4(R+1)]$.
For each point of the repeller, choose two of its four preimages
whose $z$-coordinates have opposite signs. Extending each of
them to an infinite past gives fast slopes of opposite signs,
separated by at least $|t|/[2(R+1)]$.
Hence the fast direction is history-dependent.

title: Proof
body_md:
At $t=0$, we have
$\mu_{F_{R,0}}=\mu_{p_R}\times\mu_q.$
The Ma\~n\'e--Manning formula
\cite{Manning1984,Mane1988} gives the exact dimensions
$\log2/\lambda_p$ and $\log2/\lambda_q$ of the factors,
and local dimensions add for their product.
Thus
$
 \dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_{F_{R,0}}
 =\frac{\log2}{\lambda_p}+\frac{\log2}{\lambda_q}.
$
Lemma \ref{lem:quadratic-family} also gives
$\lambda_p>\lambda_q>\log12>\log4$.

For $t\ne0$, Lemma \ref{lem:quadratic-family} gives
history dependence and
$\lambda_2(R,t)>\log12>2\log2$.
Theorem \ref{thm:mechanism} (i) therefore yields
$
\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_{F_{R,t}}
=\frac{2\log2}{\lambda_2(R,t)}>\mathcal D_{\mathrm{P}}(F_{R,t}).
$
Since $\lambda_1(R,t)=\lambda_p$ and
$\lambda_2(R,t)\to\lambda_q$ as $t\to0$, taking the limit
gives \eqref{eq:dimension-jump}.

title: Remark
body_md:
The jump
in $\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_{F_{R,t}}$ at $t=0$
reflects a change in entropy allocation.
At $t=0$, the fast leaves are horizontal,
$h_1(0)=\log2$, and $\gamma_t(0)=\log2/\lambda_q$.
For $t\ne0$, one has $h_1(t)=0$, so $\gamma_f(t)=0$ and
$$
 \gamma_t(t)=\frac{2\log2}{\lambda_2(R,t)}
 \to 2\gamma_t(0)
 \qquad\text{as }t\to0.
$$
The ratio $\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_{F_{R,t}}/\mathcal D_{\mathrm{P}}(F_{R,t})$ can approach two.
Indeed, setting $t_R:=50/R$ gives
$$
 \frac{\dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_{F_{R,t_R}}}{\mathcal D_{\mathrm{P}}(F_{R,t_R})}
 =\frac{2\lambda_1(R,t_R)}
        {\lambda_1(R,t_R)+\lambda_2(R,t_R)}
 \to 2
 \qquad\text{as }R\to\infty,
$$
since $\lambda_1(R,t_R)>\log(2(R-1))$ while
$\log12<\lambda_2(R,t_R)<\log26$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We verify the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{thm:mechanism}
by the same inverse branch and slope estimates as in
Lemma \ref{lem:quadratic-family}.
We may take $C=100$ and $B_0=10^4$.
Set $R:=\sqrt A$, $S:=\sqrt B$, and
$
 Q:=[-R-1,R+1]\times[-2S,2S]\subset\mathbb R^2.
$
The parameter conditions give $S>100$ and $10S<R<B/10$.
The four inverse branches 
of $F_{A,B}$
on $Q$ are
$g_{\sigma,\tau}$, $\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}$, given by
$$
g_{\sigma,\tau}(z,w)=(Z,W),\qquad
Z=\sigma\sqrt{A+z},\qquad
W=\tau\sqrt{B+w-Z}.
$$
They satisfy $R-1<|Z|<R+1$ and
$B/2<B+w-Z<3B/2$, so $S/\sqrt2<|W|<2S$.
As in Lemma \ref{lem:quadratic-family}, these bounds and
$\|Dg_{\sigma,\tau}\|_2<2/S<1$ give disjoint contracting branches
with images compactly contained in a small bounded convex complex
neighborhood of $Q$, and the four-branch coding identifies the
Bernoulli measure with the equilibrium measure.
The same leading homogeneous terms $(z^2,w^2)$ give the holomorphic
extension to $\mathbb P^2$.

Since $|w/z|<2S/(R-1)<1$, the same graph transform as in
Lemma \ref{lem:quadratic-family} gives a dominated fast bundle
$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}(1,s(\hat x))$ with real slope satisfying
$
|s|\le M:=\frac1{2(R-1)-4S}.
$
The slope satisfies
$s(\hat x)=1/(2z_{-1})+(w_{-1}/z_{-1})s(\hat x^-)$.
Thus \hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)} holds.
As in Lemma \ref{lem:quadratic-family}, the exponents are
the integrals of $\log|2z|$ and $\log|2w|$, giving
$
 \lambda_1>\log(2(R-1))>\log(4S)>
 \lambda_2>\log(\sqrt2 S)>\log4.
$

It remains to verify history dependence.
Since
$
|2w_{-1}s(\hat x^-)|\le4SM<\frac12,
$
the fast slope has the sign of $z_{-1}$.
Every point of the repeller has two preimages in the repeller whose
$z$-coordinates have opposite signs. Extending each of them to an
infinite past gives two histories with fast slopes of opposite signs.
The fast direction is therefore history-dependent, and
Theorem \ref{thm:mechanism} (i) gives the exact dimension
formula and the strict inequality.

label: prop:equality
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:equality}
Fix $R\ge1000$.
For real $|t|\le1$, let
$G_{R,t}(z,w):=(z^2-R^2+tw,w^2-100)$.
Then $G_{R,t}$ has a real four-branch expanding repeller
supporting its equilibrium measure.
Its fast direction is horizontal and independent of the
inverse history, and
$$
 \dim_{\mathrm H}\mu_{G_{R,t}}
 =\frac{\log2}{\lambda_1(G_{R,t})}
  +\frac{\log2}{\lambda_2(G_{R,t})}.
$$

title: Proof
body_md:
On the rectangle $Q_R$ from Section \ref{sec:jump}, the
inverse branches of $G_{R,t}$
are
$g_{\sigma,\tau}$, $\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}$, given by
$$
g_{\sigma,\tau}(z,w)=(Z,W),\qquad
W=\tau\sqrt{100+w},\qquad
Z=\sigma\sqrt{R^2+z-tW},
$$
with $9<|W|<11$ and $R-1<|Z|<R+1$.
As in Lemma \ref{lem:quadratic-family}, their disjoint,
contracting extensions to a bounded convex complex
neighborhood give a full branch repeller supporting
the equilibrium measure $\mu:=\mu_{G_{R,t}}$.

The upper triangular derivative preserves the horizontal
direction, whose expansion $|2z|>2(R-1)$ uniformly
dominates the expansion $|2w|<22$ on the vertical quotient.
Thus \hyperref[hyp:H]{(H)} holds, with horizontal fast
leaves and transverse coordinate $p_s(z,w)=w$ for every
history $s$.
The four branch Bernoulli coding gives
$
(\pi_w)_*\mu=\mu_q.
$
Consequently $\lambda_2=\lambda_q$, and the Ma\~n\'e--Manning
formula \cite{Manning1984,Mane1988} gives the exact dimension
$\log2/\lambda_2$ of $\mu_q$.

For every coordinate ball $U$ with $\mu(U)>0$, the local
transverse measure
$\zeta_U:=(\pi_w)_*\mu_U$ is absolutely continuous
with respect to $\mu_q$.
The Lebesgue differentiation theorem for finite Borel measures
shows that, for $\zeta_U$-almost every $w$, the ratio
$\zeta_U(B(w,r))/\mu_q(B(w,r))$ converges as $r\to0$ to
the positive, finite Radon--Nikodym derivative
$(d\zeta_U/d\mu_q)(w)$.
Hence $\zeta_U$ is exact dimensional of dimension
$\log2/\lambda_2$.
Proposition \ref{prop:dimension} (iii) therefore gives
$$
 \frac{2\log2-h_1}{\lambda_2}
 =\frac{\log2}{\lambda_2},
$$
so $h_1=\log2$.
Substituting into Proposition \ref{prop:dimension} (i) proves
the asserted equality.

label: lem:inverse-reduction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:inverse-reduction}
Fix two integers $m,\ell\ge1$
and three real numbers 
$0<\kappa<1$, $R_*\ge1$, and $c_0>0$.
There exists $\delta_0>0$ such that, for every $0<\delta<\delta_0$
and all sufficiently large $n$, the following holds.

$A,B\subset[-R_*,R_*]^m$ lie on the same grid.

$\omega(A)\ge1/2$
and
$2\le|B|\le2^{(1-\kappa)n}$.

$|B_a|\ge |B|^{1-\delta}$.

$$
 \left|\bigcup_{a\in A}(a+B_a)\right|
 \le |B|^{1+\delta},

$\omega(E)\ge2^{-c_0n}$ such that every $x\in E$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:unique descendant}  on at least $\kappa n/2$ scales in
$\{0,\ldots,n-\ell\}$.

label: eq:block-length-choice
title: Proof
body_md:
In this proof, the constants implicit in $O(\cdot)$
may depend
on the fixed parameters but are independent of $n$.
Set
$$
 N_m:=8\cdot2^m
 \qquad \text{and} \qquad
 \xi_T:=T^{-1}\log_2(2mT+2).
$$
Choose an integer $T$, the number of consecutive dyadic
scales in each regularization block, so large that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-length-choice}
T>4\ell(N_m+1)
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
\frac1T+\xi_T<\frac{c_0}{3}.
\end{equation}
The remaining choices are made in the order $\rho$, $\delta_0$,
and then $n$, which is taken sufficiently large.

\smallskip

\noindent {\bf Step 1: Reduction to an entropy problem.}
This step is essentially the same as in Wu's proof: the mass
decomposition, asymmetric Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers reduction, and regularization argument
carry over directly to $\mathbb R^m$, with only the bookkeeping changes
indicated in Steps 1.1--1.4.

\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 1.1: Mass decomposition
(see \cite[(4.17)--(4.18)]{Wu2025}).}
We begin exactly as in \cite{Wu2025}, 
grouping points of $A$ according to
their $\omega$-masses. The only change is the number of grid points:
a bounded $2^{-n}$-grid in $\mathbb R^m$ contains
$O_{m,R_*}(2^{mn})$ points. Hence the points of mass less than
$2^{-n(m+1/T)}$ have total mass $O_{m,R_*}(2^{-n/T})$.

Partition the remaining points according to which interval
$(2^{-(r+1)n/T},\,2^{-rn/T}]$,
$r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$,
contains their point mass $\omega(\{a\})$. At most $mT+2$
such intervals occur, and the point masses within each resulting
group vary by a factor at most $2^{n/T}$. Thus, for all
sufficiently large $n$, one such group $A_0\subset A$ satisfies
$$
 \omega(A_0)\ge c_{m,R_*,T}>0
\quad \text{and}
\quad
 2^{-n/T}
 \le
 \frac{\omega(\{a\})}{\omega(\{a'\})}
 \le
 2^{n/T},
 \quad \text{for every } a,a'\in A_0.
$$

\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 1.2: Asymmetric Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers theorem
(see \cite[(4.19)--(4.23)]{Wu2025}).}
This step is unchanged, since
\cite[Theorem 4.8]{Wu2025} holds in arbitrary additive groups.
Apply it, with the first set equal to $B$ and the second to $A_0$,
to
$$
 \mathcal G
 :=
 \{(b,a):a\in A_0,\ b\in B_a\}
 \subset B\times A_0.
$$
Set $M:=2^{(m+2)n}$. Then we have
$|B|\le M|A_0|$ and 
 $ |\mathcal G|\ge M^{-\delta}|B||A_0|$,
and the set of restricted sums has cardinality at most
$M^\delta|B|$. Therefore there are
$A'\subset A_0$ and $B'\subset B$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bsg-output}
 |A'|\ge2^{-\tau n}|A_0|,
 \qquad
 |B'|\ge2^{-\tau n}|B|,
 \qquad \text{and} \qquad
 |A'+B'|\le2^{\tau n}|B'|,
\end{equation}
where $\tau=\tau(\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\to0$.

Wu works inside $[0,1]$. To apply the regularization in Step 1.3, replace $A'$ by its intersection with a level-zero dyadic cube containing the largest number of points of $A'$.
The resulting bounded loss can be absorbed into $\tau$.
Translating the sets and $\omega$ by the negative of the
lower left corner of this cube, we may assume that the cube is
$[0,1)^m$ and that the translated dyadic partitions are
$\mathcal D_j^0$.

\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 1.3: Regularization
(see \cite[Lemma 4.9 and (4.24)--(4.28)]{Wu2025}).}
No dimensional modification is required here:
\cite[Lemma 4.9]{Wu2025} is already stated in $\mathbb R^d$.
Apply it to the uniform probability on $A'$ through
$s:=\lfloor n/T\rfloor$ blocks. We obtain
$A''\subset A'$ with
$$
 \frac{|A''|}{|A'|}
 \ge
 (2mT+2)^{-s}
 \ge
 2^{-n\xi_T}.
$$
Let $\sigma_A$ and $\sigma_B$ be the uniform probabilities on
$A''$ and $B'$, respectively.
The regularization gives numbers
$\sigma_r\in[0,m]$, $r=0,\ldots,s-1$, such that whenever
$Q$ is a level-$(r+1)T$ cube with $\sigma_A(Q)>0$ and
$\widehat Q$ is its level-$rT$ parent,
$$
 2^{-\sigma_rT-1}
 \le
 \frac{\sigma_A(Q)}{\sigma_A(\widehat Q)}
 \le
 2^{-\sigma_rT}.
$$
In particular, cubes intersecting $A''$ two block levels beneath
the same ancestor have masses within a factor four.

\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 1.4: The convolution entropy bound
(see
the end of Wu's reduction after \cite[(4.28)]{Wu2025}).}
Let $\sigma_A \ast \sigma_B$ 
denote the convolution  of 
$\sigma_A$ and $\sigma_B$, i.e., the 
push-forward of
$\sigma_A\otimes\sigma_B$ under the addition map
$(x,y)\mapsto x+y$.
Since $\sigma_A\ast\sigma_B$ is supported on
$A''+B'\subset A'+B'$,
\eqref{eq:bsg-output} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:convolution-bound}
 H(\sigma_A\ast\sigma_B,\mathcal D_n)
 \le
 \log_2|A'+B'|
 \le
 H(\sigma_B,\mathcal D_n)+\tau n.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
we have
$H(\sigma_B,\mathcal D_n)
 =
 \log_2|B'|
 \le
 (1-\kappa)n$.
Thus, in $\mathbb R^m$, we have the same entropy bounds used in \cite[(4.28)--(4.29)]{Wu2025}.

\smallskip
\noindent {\bf Step 2: From small entropy growth to point concentration.}
This is the main multidimensional modification of Wu's argument.
Hochman's inverse theorem now produces arbitrary subspaces
$V_j\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
so we must use the entropy bound on $\sigma_B$ to
show that $V_j=\{0\}$ on a positive proportion of scales.

\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 2.1: The multidimensional inverse theorem
(compare \cite[(4.29)--(4.30)]{Wu2025}).}
This is the first point where the adaptation to $\mathbb R^m$ requires a new argument.
Set
$\eta:=\kappa^2 / 100$,
so that
$\eta+\sqrt{\eta}<\kappa/4$,
and
choose $\rho>0$ sufficiently small that $\rho<2^{-2T-3}$ and $\sqrt\rho<\eta/10$.

Apply Hochman's inverse theorem
\cite[Theorem 2.8]{Hochman2017} to $\sigma_B$ as the first
measure and $\sigma_A$ as the second. After the translation in Step 1.2, both measures are supported
on $[-R,R]^m$, where $R:=2R_*+1$.
For the fixed parameters
$m,R,\rho$, and $T$, let
$\delta_H>0$ be the entropy growth threshold in the theorem.
Thus, for all sufficiently large $n$, the theorem applies whenever
\[
 H(\sigma_A\ast\sigma_B,\mathcal D_n)
 -
 H(\sigma_B,\mathcal D_n)
 <
 \delta_H n.
\]
Choose $\delta_0>0$ so small that
$\tau(\delta)<\delta_H/2$ for every $0<\delta<\delta_0$.
By 
\eqref{eq:convolution-bound},
this entropy-growth hypothesis is then satisfied.
The theorem therefore yields
subspaces
$V_j\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
such that, when $j$ is chosen uniformly
from $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ and the corresponding components are sampled independently
according to $\sigma_B$ and $\sigma_A$, the probability that the
$\sigma_B$-component is $(V_j,\rho,T)$-saturated and the
$\sigma_A$-component is $(V_j,\rho)$-concentrated is at least
$1-\rho$.

For each $j$, let $e_j$ be the probability that this joint
conclusion fails at scale $j$. Since
$$
\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^n e_j\leq\rho,
$$
Markov's inequality shows that $e_j\leq\sqrt{\rho}$ for all but at
most $\sqrt{\rho}\,n+O(1)$ scales. At each remaining scale, a set
of $\sigma_B$-mass at least $1-\sqrt{\rho}$ has
$(V_j,\rho,T)$-saturated components, while a set of
$\sigma_A$-mass at least $1-\sqrt{\rho}$ has
$(V_j,\rho)$-concentrated components.



\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 2.2: Zero subspaces at sufficiently many scales
(compare
\cite[(4.31)--(4.34)]{Wu2025}).}
In Wu's one-dimensional argument, the only possible subspaces are
$\{0\}$ and $\mathbb R$, so the entropy bound directly forces point
concentration at many scales. In $\mathbb R^m$ we must also exclude
non-zero proper
subspaces.

Hochman's local entropy average identity
\cite[Lemma 3.5]{Hochman2017} gives
$$
 \frac1nH(\sigma_B,\mathcal D_n)
 =
 \frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}
 \int
 \frac1T H(\sigma_B^{x,j},\mathcal D_T^0)
 \,d\sigma_B(x)
 +O_{m,R_*}(T/n).
$$
At each remaining scale with $V_j\ne\{0\}$, saturation implies
normalized block entropy at least $1-\rho$ on a set of
$\sigma_B$-mass at least $1-\sqrt\rho$. Hence the average
contribution of that scale is at least
 $(1-\sqrt\rho)(1-\rho)$.
Since
$H(\sigma_B,\mathcal D_n)/n\le1-\kappa$,
the number of such scales is at most
$$
 \frac{(1-\kappa)n+O_{m,R_*}(T)}
 {(1-\sqrt\rho)(1-\rho)}.
$$
By the choice of $\rho$, after accounting for the discarded
scales, we obtain at least $(\kappa-\eta)n$ scales with
$V_j=\{0\}$, for all large $n$.
At each such scale $j$, a set of $\sigma_A$-mass at least
$1-\sqrt\rho$ consists of points $x$ for which
$\sigma_A^{x,j}$ assigns mass at least $1-\rho$ to a ball
of radius $\rho$, whose center may depend on $x$ and $j$. 
This is the only new issue in the inverse theorem part compared
with Wu.

Let $J$ be the set of these scales satisfying
$j\le(s-2)T$. Then
$|J|\ge(\kappa-\eta)n-O(T)$.
For each $j\in J$, there is $F_j\subset A''$ with
$\sigma_A(F_j)\ge1-\eta$ such that, for every $x\in F_j$,
the component $\sigma_A^{x,j}$ gives mass at least $1-\eta$
to a ball of radius $\rho$.
The restriction $j\le(s-2)T$ ensures that the depth-$2T$
descendants used in Step 3.1 remain within the regularized blocks.

\smallskip
\noindent
{\bf Step 3: From point concentration to unique descendants.}
Once point concentration has been obtained, we return to Wu's
extraction argument. The only dimensional change is the branching
bound: a small ball may meet up to $2^m$ dyadic cubes, leading to
the constant $N_m=8\cdot2^m$ in place of the one-dimensional bound.


\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 3.1: The multidimensional branching bound
(compare \cite[(4.34)--(4.40)]{Wu2025}).}
Fix $j\in J$ and $x\in F_j$.
Wu's argument now extracts a bounded number of descendants from
point concentration. The only dimensional change is that a small
ball may meet several dyadic cubes.

Since $\rho<2^{-2T-3}$, the concentration ball meets at most
$2^m$ cubes at relative depth $2T$. Hence some
level-$(j+2T)$ descendant
$Q_*\subset\mathcal D_j(x)$ satisfies
$\sigma_A(Q_*)
 \ge
 (1-\eta)2^{-m}\sigma_A(\mathcal D_j(x))$.
Set
$r:=\lfloor j/T\rfloor+1$,
so that $rT$ is the first block level strictly greater than $j$.
Since $(r+1)T\le j+2T$, the level-$(r+1)T$ ancestor $Q^*$
of $Q_*$ satisfies
$ \sigma_A(Q^*)\ge\sigma_A(Q_*)$.

All level-$(r+1)T$ cubes inside $\mathcal D_j(x)$ which meet
$A''$ share the level-$(r-1)T$ ancestor of $x$.
By the two-block comparison from Step 1.3, each such cube $Q$
satisfies
$$
 \sigma_A(Q)
 \ge
 \frac14\sigma_A(Q^*)
 \ge
 \frac{1-\eta}{4\cdot2^m}
 \sigma_A(\mathcal D_j(x)).
$$
They are disjoint, so their number is at most
$(4\cdot2^m)/(1-\eta)
 \le
 N_m=8\cdot2^m$.
This is the multidimensional counterpart of the bound on the number
of occupied descendant intervals in \cite[(4.40)]{Wu2025}.

\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 3.2: Unique descendant scales
(see \cite[(4.41)--(4.45)]{Wu2025}).}
From this point Wu's tree argument is unchanged, with $N_m$
in place of the one-dimensional branching bound.

Along the chain of dyadic cubes containing $x$, call a level
\emph{branching} if the cube has at least two immediate children
meeting $A''$. Between levels $rT$ and $(r+1)T-1$, there are at
most $N_m-1$ branching levels, since each branching creates an
additional level-$(r+1)T$ descendant meeting $A''$.
Each branching level can make the unique descendant property fail
for at most $\ell$ starting scales. Allowing also for windows
crossing the end of the block, at least
 $T-\ell N_m-\ell$
 starting scales in this block have the unique descendant property
relative to $A''$.

We now select points for which this happens in sufficiently many
blocks, exactly as in Wu's passage from (4.42) to (4.45).
Since
$$
 \int
 \#\{j\in J:x\notin F_j\}
 \,d\sigma_A(x)
 \le
 \eta n,
$$
Markov's inequality gives $E\subset A''$ with
$\sigma_A(E)\ge1-\sqrt\eta$ such that every $x\in E$ belongs to
$F_j$ for at least
 $(\kappa-\eta-\sqrt\eta)n-O(T)$
indices $j\in J$.
At most $T$ indices $j$ correspond to the same following block
$[rT,(r+1)T)$. Hence every $x\in E$ has at least
$
 (\kappa-\eta-\sqrt\eta)n/{T} -O(1)$
good following blocks. By \eqref{eq:block-length-choice} and our choice of $\eta$,
we have
$$
T-\ell N_m-\ell>\frac{3T}{4}
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
\eta+\sqrt\eta<\frac{\kappa}{4}.
$$
Thus, for all large $n$, every $x\in E$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:unique descendant} 
on at least
$\kappa n/2$ scales.
Indeed, since $E\subset A''$, at most one level-$(j+\ell)$
descendant can meet $E$; the descendant containing $x$ does
meet $E$, since $x\in E$.

\smallskip
\noindent
\emph{Step 3.3: Returning to the original measure
(compare the estimates
after \cite[(4.46)]{Wu2025}).}
It remains to show that $E$ has sufficiently large $\omega$-mass.

Since $\sigma_A$ is uniform on $A''$ and
$\sigma_A(E)\ge1-\sqrt\eta>1/2$, we have
$|E|\ge|A''|/2$.
The point masses of $\omega$ on $A_0$ differ by at most
$2^{n/T}$, hence
$$
 \omega(E)
 \ge
 2^{-n/T}\frac{|E|}{|A_0|}\omega(A_0).
$$
Using \eqref{eq:bsg-output}, 
$ {|A'|}/{|A_0|}\ge2^{-\tau n}$,
and the regularization estimate
$ {|A''|}/{|A'|}\ge2^{-n\xi_T}$,
we obtain
$$
 \omega(E)
 \ge
 C_{m,R_*,T}^{-1}
 2^{-n(1/T+\tau+\xi_T)}.
$$
By 
the second condition in
\eqref{eq:block-length-choice}, after shrinking $\delta_0$
further so that $\tau<c_0/3$, we have
$1/T+\tau+\xi_T<2c_0/3$.
For all sufficiently large $n$ this gives
$\omega(E)\ge2^{-c_0n}$.
Undoing the translation from Step 1.2 gives a subset $E$ of the
original $A$, with the same unique descendant counts and $\omega$-mass bound.
This proves the assertion.

body_md:
We first prove (i). The case $|B|=1$ is immediate. Let $c>0$
be given by Lemma \ref{lem:pruning}. Apply
Lemma \ref{lem:inverse-reduction} with $c_0=c/2$ and let
$\delta_0>0$ be the resulting constant. Set
$\delta:=\delta_0/2$.
After increasing the lower bound on $n$ if necessary, both
Lemmas \ref{lem:pruning} and \ref{lem:inverse-reduction} apply.

Suppose that (i) fails. Then
$|\Sigma|\le |B|^{1+\delta}$.
Lemma \ref{lem:inverse-reduction} gives a set $E\subset A$ such
that
$\omega(E)\ge 2^{-cn/2}$
and every $x\in E$ satisfies the unique descendant property
\eqref{eq:unique descendant}  on at least $\kappa n/2$ scales in
$\{0,\ldots,n-\ell\}$. Lemma \ref{lem:pruning} then gives
$\omega(E)\le 2^{-cn}$, which gives 
a contradiction for all sufficiently large $n$. This proves (i).

\smallskip

We now prove (ii). 
Let $Z$ satisfy the approximation
hypothesis 
of part (ii),
and cover $Z$ by $N_{2^{-n}}(Z)$ balls of radius $2^{-n}$. 
For every $a\in A$ and $b\in B_a$, the corresponding
sum $a+b\in\Sigma$ lies within distance $C_0 2^{-n}$ of a point
of $Z$. Hence the balls with the same centers and radius
$(C_0+1)2^{-n}$ cover $\Sigma$.
Since $A$ and $B$ lie on the same translated $2^{-n}$-grid,
$\Sigma$ lies on a translate of $2^{-n}\mathbb Z^m$. Each ball
of radius $(C_0+1)2^{-n}$ therefore contains at most
$C(m,C_0)$ points of $\Sigma$. It follows that
$|\Sigma|
 \le C(m,C_0) N_{2^{-n}}(Z)$.
Using (i), we obtain
$N_{2^{-n}}(Z)
 \ge c(m,C_0)|\Sigma|
 \ge c(m,C_0)|B|^{1+\delta}$, which
 proves (ii).
